lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1814, a street in London was hit by a wave of beer.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: At the Horse Shoe Brewery on Tottenham Court Road, a giant wooden vat of dark porter stood more than twenty feet tall.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That afternoon, one of the iron hoops holding it together slipped off. A clerk was told not to worry about it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: About an hour later, the vat burst.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It smashed open the vats around it, and more than a million litres of beer tore through the brewery's back wall.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: A wave of beer around fifteen feet high poured into the slum of St Giles.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Whole families there lived in cellars. The beer poured straight in.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Eight people died. Some were mourners at a little boy's wake. One was a fourteen-year-old barmaid, buried when a wall came down.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: Okay. I thought this was going to be a funny one.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: You might have heard that crowds rushed out to drink it. The newspapers of the time don't say that. They describe neighbours digging through the rubble for survivors.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: At the inquest, the jury called it an act of God. The brewery paid nothing, and even got the tax on its lost beer refunded.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The brewery kept going for another hundred years. Today, a theatre stands on the spot. Subscribe for more.
